details:
**Genghis Khan (Temujin)**
The founder of the Mongol Empire, born Temujin, who united the steppe tribes and was proclaimed Genghis Khan at a kurultai in 1206. His conquests began what became the largest contiguous land empire in history. The giveaway in most Mongol questions.

**Kublai Khan and the Yuan dynasty**
Genghis's grandson Kublai founded the Yuan dynasty in China, ruled from Khanbaliq (modern Beijing), and hosted Marco Polo. The Yuan circulated paper money called chao and finished off the Southern Song in 1279, after the siege of Xiangyang and the naval Battle of Yamen. The dynasty fell after the Red Turban Rebellion, when Zhu Yuanzhang became the Hongwu Emperor of the Ming.

**Kamikaze ("divine wind")**
The typhoons that wrecked Kublai Khan's two invasion fleets against Japan, in 1274 and 1281, helping the Kamakura shogunate repel the Mongols. Other failed Yuan expeditions include the defeat by the Vietnamese at the Bach Dang River, where wooden stakes were planted in the riverbed to wreck the Mongol fleet, and the expedition to Java against King Kertanegara, in which their ally Raden Wijaya turned on them.

**Hulagu and the sack of Baghdad (1258)**
Hulagu, a grandson of Genghis and founder of the Ilkhanate in Persia, sacked Abbasid Baghdad and executed the last caliph, al-Musta'sim, by rolling him in a rug and trampling him with horses. Legend says so many books from the Grand Library (House of Wisdom) were thrown into the Tigris that the river ran black with ink.

**Battle of Ain Jalut (1260)**
The battle in Palestine where the Egyptian Mamluks defeated a Mongol army, halting Mongol expansion into the Middle East. It was one of the first major defeats of the Mongols.

**Golden Horde**
The westernmost Mongol successor state, also called the Kipchak Khanate or Ulus of Jochi. It was founded by Batu Khan, ruled from Sarai, and dominated the Russian principalities for over two centuries. Its name may come from the color or gleam of its tents.

**Battle of Kulikovo and the Great Stand on the Ugra**
At Kulikovo in 1380, Grand Prince Dmitri Ivanovich of Moscow defeated the Golden Horde's general Mamai, earning the name "Donskoy." The 1480 Great Stand on the Ugra River, a standoff that ended without a battle, marked the end of the "Tatar yoke" over Russia.

**Siege of Caffa and the Black Death**
During the 1346 siege of the Genoese trading city of Caffa in Crimea, Golden Horde forces allegedly catapulted plague-ridden corpses over the walls. Fleeing Genoese ships are often blamed for carrying the Black Death to Europe.

**Kurultai**
The assembly of Mongol nobles that chose new khans and decided major policy, which elite women such as Genghis's wife Borte attended. A kurultai proclaimed Temujin as Genghis Khan in 1206.

**Mongol military organization (tumen, keshig, mangudai)**
The Mongol army was organized by tens, with units of 1,000 (mingghan) and 10,000 (tumen) soldiers. The khan was protected by an imperial guard called the keshig, divided into day and night shifts, and the army used light cavalry called mangudai, horse archers with composite bows and thumb rings, and tactics like the feigned retreat.

**Oirats and the Tumu Crisis**
The Oirats were a western Mongol confederation (the "Four Oirat"). In the 1449 Tumu Crisis, the Oirat leader Esen captured the Ming emperor Zhengtong (Yingzong). Their descendants include the Kalmyks of the lower Volga region of Russia.

**Ögedei and Karakorum**
Ögedei, Genghis's son and successor as Great Khan, built the Mongol capital at Karakorum. During his reign, Mongol armies invaded Europe, winning the 1241 Battles of Legnica (over Henry the Pious of Silesia) and Mohi (over Béla IV of Hungary).

**Pax Mongolica and the yam**
The relative peace and security across the Mongol Empire that let trade and ideas move freely along the Silk Road. It was supported by the yam, a relay system of postal stations for messengers similar to the Pony Express. The historian Marie Favereau compared this exchange to the Columbian Exchange.

**Keraites, Nestorian Christianity, and Rabban Bar Sauma**
The Keraites were a Mongol-era steppe tribe that had converted to Nestorian Christianity, and their ruler Toghrul was linked to the legend of Prester John. Rabban Bar Sauma, a Nestorian monk from Yuan China, traveled to Europe as an Ilkhanate envoy seeking an alliance with France and the Pope against the Mamluks.

**Baron Ungern-Sternberg, Sukhbaatar, and modern Mongolia**
After Mongolia broke from the Qing in 1911 under the Bogd Khan, the White Russian warlord Baron Roman von Ungern-Sternberg seized Urga in 1921. He was defeated by Soviet and Mongolian forces including Damdin Sükhbaatar, whose name ("hero") is part of the name of the modern capital, Ulaanbaatar ("Red Hero").
